questions.text: The Battle of Panipat in 1526 established Mughal rule in India. Babur defeated ____.

options.text: Ibrahim Lodi — the last Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate
Rana Sanga — the powerful Rajput ruler and king of Mewar
Sher Shah Suri — Afghan ruler who controlled northern India
Hemu Vikramaditya — Hindu general who briefly captured Delhi

questions.explanation: First Battle of Panipat (1526): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate (Lodi dynasty), ending the Sultanate era and founding the Mughal Empire. Rana Sanga was defeated at the Battle of Khanwa (1527). Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun (not Babur). Hemu was defeated at Second Panipat (1556) by Akbar.

questions.text: Akbar's Mansabdari system was a key administrative innovation. In this system, Mansabdars were ____.

options.text: ranked officials who held both civil and military responsibilities
hereditary landlords who collected revenue from fixed territories
religious scholars who administered Islamic law in Mughal courts
merchant guilds who managed the Mughal empire's trade networks

questions.explanation: Mansabdars were ranked officials (mansab = rank) with two numerical designations: zat (personal rank/salary) and sawar (number of horsemen to maintain). They served in both civil and military capacities and could be transferred anywhere — preventing local loyalty buildup. Ranks were NOT hereditary, unlike Zamindar land rights.

questions.text: Akbar's revenue system, developed with his finance minister Todar Mal, was called the ____.

options.text: Zabt (Dahsala) system — based on 10-year average crop yield and prices
Ryotwari system — direct settlement between state and individual farmers
Zamindari system — revenue collected through hereditary local landlords
Muqaddami system — village headmen assessed and collected taxes collectively

questions.explanation: Todar Mal's Dahsala (ten-yearly) or Zabt system: land measured, crop yields and prices averaged over 10 years to fix a standard revenue assessment. It was systematic, measurement-based, and reduced arbitrary extortion. Ryotwari (direct farmer settlement) and Zamindari (landlord intermediary) are 19th-century British land revenue systems.

questions.text: Aurangzeb's reimposition of jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims) in 1679 reversed Akbar's religious policy. Jizya was ____.

options.text: a tax levied on non-Muslim subjects in lieu of military service
a tax levied on Muslim pilgrims travelling to Mecca
a general agricultural tax paid by all subjects of the empire
a tariff on luxury goods imported into the Mughal empire

questions.explanation: Jizya was a protection tax levied on dhimmis (non-Muslim subjects) under Islamic law, historically in lieu of military service (from which they were exempt). Akbar abolished it in 1564 as part of his sulh-i-kul (universal peace) policy. Aurangzeb's reimposition in 1679 alienated the Hindu nobility and contributed to Rajput and Maratha rebellions.

questions.text: The Mughal architectural style reached its zenith during Shah Jahan's reign. Which of the following is NOT associated with Shah Jahan?

options.text: Taj Mahal — built as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal
Red Fort (Lal Qila), Delhi — his new capital built at Shahjahanabad
Fatehpur Sikri — a new capital city built near Agra
Jama Masjid, Delhi — the largest mosque in India at the time

questions.explanation: Fatehpur Sikri was built by AKBAR (not Shah Jahan) as his capital near Agra, around 1571, later abandoned due to water scarcity. Taj Mahal (1632–53), Red Fort/Shahjahanabad (1639), and Jama Masjid Delhi (1656) are all Shah Jahan's constructions. Shah Jahan's reign is considered the golden age of Mughal architecture.

questions.text: The Mughal emperor who commissioned the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari — detailed accounts of Akbar's reign — was ____.

options.text: Akbar himself — who patronised Abu'l-Fazl to write these accounts
Jahangir — who wrote his own memoirs Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri
Humayun — who commissioned them to legitimise Mughal succession
Shah Jahan — who wanted a comprehensive history of the dynasty

questions.explanation: Akbar patronised his court historian Abu'l-Fazl ibn Mubarak to write the Akbarnama (chronicle of Akbar's reign) and Ain-i-Akbari (administration, culture, statistics of the empire). Jahangir wrote his own memoirs (Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri). Babur wrote the Baburnama. These are primary Mughal literary-historical sources studied for UPSC and banking exams.

questions.text: The Maratha confederacy under the Peshwas posed the greatest challenge to late Mughal authority. The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was fought between ____.

options.text: The Marathas and Ahmad Shah Durrani (Afghan); Marathas suffered a crushing defeat
The Marathas and the British East India Company for control of the Deccan
Maratha forces and a weakened late-Mughal emperor's army for control of Delhi
Ahmad Shah Durrani and the Sikh confederacy for control of the Punjab region

questions.explanation: Third Panipat (14 January 1761): The Marathas (under Vishwasrao and Bhau Sahib, representing Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao) were decisively defeated by Ahmad Shah Durrani (Abdali) of Afghanistan. This destroyed Maratha expansionism into North India, allowed British hegemony to grow, and shattered the Peshwa confederacy's prestige. The battle killed ~100,000 Marathas.
